subject: How to get p values for all the observe variables of the latent variables

messages.author: 625ec39184b7e7ce
messages.subject: How to get p values for all the observe variables of the latent variables
parts:
Dear experts:
I have a model with one latent variable (brainbeta)with two observed variables (combined7 combined8). From the output graph, one observed variable seemed to have a significant contribution (p<0.05), with a number printed out on the link between the latent variable and the observed variable (combined7).  While the output table showed one observed variable (combined7) had a factor loading of 1 (default I guess) and no p-value reported, and the second observed variable (combined8) has p value reported (factor loading of 0.29). 

Latent Variables:
                             Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|) ci.lower  ci.upper   Std.lv  Std.all
  BrainBeta =~                                                                            
    combined7         1.000                                                1.000    1.000   11.373    1.396
    combined8         0.297    0.390    0.761    0.447    -0.468    1.062    3.377    0.313

1.How can I get the p-value of variable combined7?
2. I want to make the conclusion of variable combined7 contributes more than B to the latent variable. If P value of combined7 is significant while combined8 is not, I guess the conclusion is reasonable. If I couldn't get the p value for some reason, can I compare the factor loading (1>0.29) to make a such conclusion?
3. What coefficient should I report in a paper? The Estimate,  Std.lv, or Std.all? Is there a reference paper (ideally not a theoretical paper)I can refer to about what to report in SEM
Thanks very much for your help

messages.author: ad188126f9138663
messages.subject: Re: How to get p values for all the observe variables of the latent variables
parts:
Xiao,
Let's begin with your path diagram.  You appear to have a double-headed arrow between L and V2.  Double headed arrows are normally curved to clearly distinguish them from single-headed arrows.  Both L and V2 are on the receiving end of single-headed arrows, indicating that they are endogenous variables.  As such, your double-headed arrow does not represent a covariance between L and V2 but rather a covariance between their disturbances.  This is more explicit in LISREL style path diagrams and requires more knowledge on the part of the reader in RAM style path diagrams such as yours.  Also, you have omitted the variances from your diagram but presumably they are all there implicitly.  If that comports with your understanding of the diagram, then we are on the same page.

It seems to me that your hypothesis about the factor loadings (which can also be interpreted or even re-parameterized as effect coefficients) is unrelated to V1 and V2 because these are causes of L, not effects of L.  That suggests a simple solution.  Drop V1 and V2 from the analysis used to test the hypothesis of equal loadings.  Instead of fixing the value of one loading, instead fix the variance of L to 1.  (Any introductory SEM text will explain why some such constraint is necessary.)  Then fit two models: one with the two loadings estimated as separate parameters and one exactly the same but with an equality constraint between the two loadings.  The chi-square difference test between fit of the two models will test the null hypothesis that the loadings are equal.  If you reject this hypothesis and the estimated loadings differ in the expected direction, then that would support your hypothesis.

This is preferable to your proposed analytic strategy for the following reason.  Inferential statistics only tell us what we have sufficient information to reject according to a predetermined decision making rule.  They cannot tell us what is true about the population.  As a result,  it does not follow from zero falling inside the confidence interval for one parameter an not another that we can reject the hypothesis of equality between the two parameters. It is better to directly test your hypothesis about the equality of the two.

See the model.syntax help file and the lavaan tutorial (online) for details on how to implement the models described above.  After you test your hypothesis with a CFA model, you can add V1 and V2 back in to estimate the remaining parameters.  In that model, it will be easiest to place constraints on the loadings because the variances of L will no longer be a parameter in the model.  It will be determined by other parameters.  This is not your only option but I believe that it is the simplest option that meets your needs.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: How to get p values for all the observe variables of the latent variables
parts:
Xiao,
It occurred to me after I hit "post" that you may run into identification problems with two indicators.  Here is a better option.  Fix the variance of L to zero as above but include V1 and V2 with covariances between V1, V2 and L (all three).  Then, as a second model, constrain the two loadings to equal one another as suggested above and compare the fit of the two models.

Keith
